::: {.objectives}
#### Learning objectives

* Build subcellular spatial maps of classification results with `plot2D`, and
  compare different dimensionality reduction methods (`plot2Dmethods`).
* Pre-compute PCA, t-SNE, UMAP and LDA coordinates (`plot = FALSE`) and reuse
  them (`method = "none"`) for efficient, reproducible figures.
* Find proteins of interest, such as members of a protein complex, with
  `pRolocVis`, and highlight them on spatial maps (`highlightOnPlot`).
* Add your own annotations, such as complexes, pathways or compartments left
  out of training, as new `fData` columns and plot them.
* Show the confidence of organellar predictions on a spatial map by scaling
  points by their probability.
* Check classification results critically by plotting both maps and profiles
  of classified proteins, and refine markers again where needed.
:::




## Introduction

In the previous lesson we classified the proteins in our U-2 OS data using an
SVM and TAGM-MAP, and generated our first spatial maps. Our `msn` object now
contains the curated markers (`markers`) and the thresholded predictions of
both classifiers (`svm.pred` and `tagm.map.allocation.pred`).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Columns we will use in this lesson
msn |>
  fvarLabels()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "Channel"                  "Decoy"                   
 [3] "Proteotypic"              "Protein.Ids"             
 [5] "Protein.Group"            "Protein.Names"           
 [7] "Genes"                    "PG.TopN"                 
 [9] "Genes.TopN"               "Translated.Q.Value"      
[11] "Channel.Q.Value"          "Lib.PG.Q.Value"          
[13] "is_contaminant"           "hc"                      
[15] "hdb_cluster_id"           "hdb_cluster_prob"        
[17] "markers_initial"          "markers"                 
[19] "svm"                      "svm.scores"              
[21] "svm.pred"                 "tagm.map.allocation"     
[23] "tagm.map.probability"     "tagm.map.outlier"        
[25] "overall_prob"             "tagm.map.allocation.pred"
```


:::
:::


In this lesson we look at how to get the most out of these results through
visualisation: making spatial maps efficiently with different dimensionality
reduction methods, overlaying proteins and annotations of interest, showing the
confidence of predictions, and checking the results critically.


## Spatial maps with different dimensionality reduction methods

Regardless of the algorithm used, the result of classification is a list of
proteins and their predicted subcellular localisations. These can be
visualised as a "subcellular spatial map" using `plot2D`, by passing the
column containing the thresholded predictions to `fcol`. In the previous
lesson we used PCA, the default. However, `plot2D` supports several other
methods, listed in `plot2Dmethods` (see `?plot2D` for details).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot2Dmethods
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "PCA"    "MDS"    "kpca"   "lda"    "t-SNE"  "UMAP"   "nipals" "hexbin"
 [9] "none"   "scree" 
```


:::
:::


Each method summarises the data in a different way, and no single method shows
everything. As discussed in the lesson on assessing resolution, PCA preserves
distances but only shows two components at a time, whereas non-linear methods
such as t-SNE and UMAP often separate clusters more clearly but distort
distances. It is therefore good practice to look at more than one.

### Pre-computing coordinates

Non-linear methods such as t-SNE and UMAP can take from a minute to tens of
minutes to compute on a dataset of this size. They are also stochastic, so
each run gives a slightly different picture unless we set a seed. Rather than
recomputing the coordinates every time we make a plot, it is good practice to
compute them once, with a seed, and reuse them.

To do this, we pass `plot = FALSE` to `plot2D`. Instead of drawing a plot,
`plot2D` then returns a matrix of the two-dimensional coordinates of each
protein. Below we pre-compute coordinates for PCA, UMAP, t-SNE and linear
discriminant analysis (LDA). LDA is a supervised method: it uses the markers
to find the projection that best separates the compartments.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## PCA is deterministic, so we do not need to set a seed
pcas <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "PCA", plot = FALSE)

## UMAP
set.seed(399)
umap <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "UMAP", plot = FALSE)

## t-SNE
set.seed(399)
tsne <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "t-SNE", plot = FALSE)

## Linear discriminant analysis (uses the markers column)
set.seed(399)
lda <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "lda", plot = FALSE)
```
:::




Each object is a matrix with one row per protein and two columns.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
head(pcas)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
           PC1 (35.15%) PC2 (25.23%)
A0A096LP01    -2.811345   -5.2274624
A0A0B4J2F0    -2.377583   -5.4941955
A0A3B3IRV3     2.425945    1.4670772
A0A3B3IS91     5.156840   -0.3892221
A0AV96         4.093129    0.5750826
A0AVF1         4.644023   -0.2817537
```


:::
:::


### Plotting pre-computed coordinates

We can now pass these coordinates back to `plot2D` with `method = "none"`,
which tells `plot2D` not to compute anything. Because a matrix of coordinates
does not contain the feature data, we also pass our `MSnSet` to `methargs` so
that `plot2D` knows where to find the `fcol` annotation. Here we visualise the
SVM results with all four methods.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA")
plot2D(umap, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "UMAP")
plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "t-SNE")
plot2D(lda, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "LDA")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "svm.pred", where = "topright", ncol = 2, cex = .7)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


The same compartments are found in all four maps, but each method shows them
differently. Compartments that overlap in the PCA plot may be clearly separated
in the t-SNE or UMAP plots, and vice versa. Remember that distances between
clusters in t-SNE and UMAP plots cannot be interpreted directly.

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Comparing classifiers across methods
{{< level 1 >}}

Using the pre-computed coordinates, plot the TAGM-MAP results
(`fcol = "tagm.map.allocation.pred"`) next to the SVM results for one of the
non-linear methods (UMAP or t-SNE). Do the differences between the two
classifiers that we saw on the PCA plot in the previous lesson also appear
here?

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot2D(umap, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "UMAP: SVM")
plot2D(umap, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "tagm.map.allocation.pred", main = "UMAP: TAGM-MAP")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "tagm.map.allocation.pred",
          where = "topright", cex = .6)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=1152}
:::
:::


As on the PCA plot, TAGM-MAP classifies more proteins than the SVM, and the
additional proteins lie mostly at the edges of clusters and in the regions
between them.

:::
:::


## Overlaying features of interest

Users may wish to add additional information to their maps, for example small
protein complexes, pathways of interest, or compartments that were not used as
training data because they lacked resolution or had too few marker proteins.
If the aim of the experiment is to produce as comprehensive a map as possible
for the community, it is important to add these other layers of information
where they are available.

### Finding proteins of interest with `pRolocVis`

The `pRolocVis` function from the `pRolocGUI` package provides a searchable
version of our feature data alongside an interactive spatial map.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Open pRolocGUI with the SVM results
pRolocVis(msn, fcol = "svm.pred")
```
:::


In the "Table Selection" tab, we can choose which columns of the feature data
to display, for example a column of gene names or protein descriptions and the
`svm.pred` column. Use `fvarLabels(msn)` to see which columns are available
in your data. We can then search the table in the "Spatial Map" tab, for
example by gene name, to find the proteins of interest and see where they lie
on the map. Note that searching relies on the information contained in the
feature data: if a column of gene names or descriptions is not available, it
can be added from databases such as UniProt.

Here, we look at two protein complexes: (1) the WASH complex, which activates
the Arp2/3 complex and is involved in actin polymerisation at endosomes, and
(2) the RNA exosome complex, which degrades RNA in the nucleus and cytoplasm.
Having identified the UniProt accessions of the members of each complex, we
store them as character vectors.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## UniProt accessions of members of each complex
wash <- c("Q12768", "Q2M389", "Q641Q2", "Q9NQA3", "Q9Y3C0", "Q9Y4E1")

exosome <- c("Q06265", "Q13868", "Q15024", "Q5RKV6", "Q96B26",
             "Q9NPD3", "Q9NQT4", "Q9NQT5", "Q9Y2L1", "Q9Y3B2")
```
:::


Not every protein in a complex will necessarily be quantified in our
experiment, so we first check which ones are present in our data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Keep only the proteins quantified in our data
wash <- intersect(wash, featureNames(msn))
exosome <- intersect(exosome, featureNames(msn))

length(wash)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 6
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
length(exosome)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 10
```


:::
:::


### Highlighting proteins on a map with `highlightOnPlot`

The `highlightOnPlot` function adds points for selected proteins on top of an
existing spatial map. We first draw the map with `plot2D`, and then pass the
same coordinates (here `pcas`) and our proteins of interest (`foi`, features
of interest) to `highlightOnPlot`, along with arguments controlling the
appearance of the points.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Spatial map of the SVM results
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA: WASH and exosome complexes")

## Highlight the complexes
highlightOnPlot(pcas, foi = wash, col = "black", bg = "grey",
                pch = 24, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)
highlightOnPlot(pcas, foi = exosome, col = "red", bg = "white",
                pch = 22, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)

## Legend for the compartments
addLegend(msn, fcol = "svm.pred", where = "topright", cex = .6)

## Legend for the complexes
legend("topleft", legend = c("WASH", "Exosome"),
       col = c("black", "red"), pt.bg = c("grey", "white"),
       pch = c(24, 22), bty = "n", cex = .8)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


Because the coordinates are pre-computed, we can highlight the same proteins
on any of the other maps simply by replacing `pcas` with `umap`, `tsne` or
`lda`.

### Adding annotations as a new `fData` column

Alternatively, we can store our annotations in a new column of the feature
data, just as we did for markers. This keeps the annotation with the data and
allows us to use all the usual plotting functions. The easiest way is to
create a named vector, with the annotation as values and the protein
accessions as names, and add it with `addMarkers`. All proteins not in the
vector are labelled `"unknown"`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Named vector of complex annotations
complexes <- c(setNames(rep("WASH complex", length(wash)), wash),
               setNames(rep("Exosome complex", length(exosome)), exosome))

## Add as a new fData column called "complexes"
msn <- addMarkers(msn, markers = complexes, mcol = "complexes")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Markers in data: 16 out of 8736
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
organelleMarkers
Exosome complex         unknown    WASH complex 
             10            8720               6 
```


:::
:::


We can now pass this column to `fcol` to plot a map in which only our
proteins of interest are coloured.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Plot map with proteins coloured by complex
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "complexes", main = "PCA: protein complexes")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "complexes", where = "topleft", cex = .8)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The same approach can be used for any annotation, for example proteins from a
pathway of interest, proteins identified in another experiment, or a
compartment that was not included in the training data.

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Where do your favourite proteins localise?
{{< level 2 >}}

Choose a small set of proteins you are interested in, for example the members
of another protein complex or a few proteins from your own research. You can
find their UniProt accessions using `pRolocVis` or the UniProt website.

1. Check which of them are present in `msn`.
2. Highlight them on the t-SNE or UMAP map of the SVM results using
   `highlightOnPlot`.
3. Look up their predicted localisation in the `svm.pred` and
   `tagm.map.allocation.pred` columns. Do the two classifiers agree? Does the
   result match what you would expect from the literature?

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}

Here we use three subunits of the proteasome as an example. Replace the
accessions with your own proteins of interest.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Example proteins of interest
my_proteins <- c("P25786", "P25787", "P28066")

## 1. Which are present in the data?
my_proteins <- intersect(my_proteins, featureNames(msn))
my_proteins
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "P25786" "P25787" "P28066"
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## 2. Highlight them on the t-SNE map
plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "t-SNE: my proteins")
highlightOnPlot(tsne, foi = my_proteins, col = "black", bg = "yellow",
                pch = 21, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## 3. Predicted localisations from both classifiers
fData(msn)[my_proteins, c("markers", "svm.pred", "tagm.map.allocation.pred")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
          markers   svm.pred tagm.map.allocation.pred
P25786 Proteasome Proteasome               Proteasome
P25787 Proteasome Proteasome               Proteasome
P28066    unknown Proteasome                  unknown
```


:::
:::


If a protein of interest is itself a marker, its prediction simply reflects
its marker annotation.

:::
:::


## Showing the confidence of predictions

A spatial map coloured by predicted compartment shows *where* proteins are
assigned, but not *how confident* we are in each assignment. One way to show
this is to scale the size of each point by its score or probability, so that
confident predictions appear as large points and uncertain ones as small
points. The `plot2D` function accepts a vector of point sizes through its
`cex` argument.

Here we scale the points of the TAGM-MAP map by the `overall_prob` column we
created in the previous lesson (the localisation probability multiplied by one
minus the outlier probability). We use the full TAGM-MAP allocation
(`tagm.map.allocation`), before thresholding, so that every protein is
coloured by its most probable compartment.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Point size based on the overall TAGM-MAP probability
ptsze <- exp(fData(msn)$overall_prob) - 1

plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "tagm.map.allocation", cex = ptsze,
       main = "PCA: TAGM-MAP allocations, sized by probability")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "tagm.map.allocation", where = "topright", cex = .6)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


Proteins near the centre of a cluster appear as large points, whereas proteins
with a low probability, or a high probability of being an outlier, shrink
towards nothing. Notice, however, how few points are small. As we saw in the
previous lesson, the TAGM-MAP probabilities are very close to 0 or 1 for most
proteins, so even proteins lying between compartments often appear with full
size.

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Confidence of the SVM predictions
{{< level 1 >}}

Make the same plot for the SVM, using the `svm` column for colour and the
`svm.scores` column for point size. How does the picture compare with the
TAGM-MAP plot?

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Point size based on the SVM score
ptsze_svm <- exp(fData(msn)$svm.scores) - 1

plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm", cex = ptsze_svm,
       main = "PCA: SVM classifications, sized by score")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "svm", where = "topright", cex = .6)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


Because the SVM scores are spread more evenly between 0 and 1, the point sizes
vary much more. Proteins at the edges of clusters and between compartments
appear as small points, giving a more graded picture of confidence than the
TAGM-MAP probabilities.

:::
:::


## Verifying the results of protein localisation classification

As discussed in the data annotation lesson, the curation of markers and their
use for classification is an iterative process. Having completed
classification, we should check whether the results look realistic and
whether each compartment is accurately represented. In particular, we should
plot (1) maps and (2) profiles of the classified proteins, using more than one
dimensionality reduction method.

As an example, we return to the difference we saw between the two classifiers
in the previous lesson: TAGM-MAP assigned many more proteins to the ER than the
SVM. Do the profiles of these additional proteins look like those of the ER
markers? To answer this, we extract the proteins classified as ER by TAGM-MAP
but left as `"unknown"` by the SVM.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Proteins assigned to the ER by TAGM-MAP but not by the SVM
er_extra <- msn |>
  fData() |>
  filter(markers == "unknown",
         tagm.map.allocation.pred == "ER",
         svm.pred == "unknown") |>
  rownames()

length(er_extra)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 801
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
## ER marker proteins
er_markers <- featureNames(msn)[fData(msn)$markers == "ER"]
```
:::


We can now plot the profiles of these proteins together with the ER markers
using `plotDist`. The `markers` argument tells `plotDist` which proteins to
highlight, here the ER markers in orange, while the additional proteins are
plotted in grey.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Profiles of the additional ER proteins (grey) and the ER markers (orange)
plotDist(msn[c(er_extra, er_markers), ],
         markers = er_markers, type = "l",
         mcol = "darkorange", pcol = "grey",
         las = 2)
title("ER markers (orange) and additional TAGM-MAP ER proteins (grey)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


We can also highlight these proteins on the maps.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA")
highlightOnPlot(pcas, foi = er_extra, col = "black", pch = 1, cex = .8)

plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "t-SNE")
highlightOnPlot(tsne, foi = er_extra, col = "black", pch = 1, cex = .8)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=1152}
:::
:::


If the additional proteins have profiles similar to those of the ER markers
and lie close to the ER cluster in several maps, they may well be genuine ER
proteins that the SVM was too conservative to assign. If, instead, their
profiles differ and they lie between clusters, they are more likely to be
proteins with mixed or uncertain localisation that TAGM-MAP has assigned with
overconfidence.

Checks such as these may reveal problems with the classification that lead us
back to the markers. For example, a compartment that absorbs many proteins
from between clusters may have markers that are too spread out, or a
compartment that is consistently under-represented may need more markers. As
discussed in the data annotation lesson, any changes should be made with care
and recorded, and should keep the markers representative of the data and the
literature.

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Checking another compartment
{{< level 2 >}}

Repeat the check above for chromatin, the other compartment where TAGM-MAP
assigned many more proteins than the SVM. Do the additional proteins look like
the chromatin markers?

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Proteins assigned to chromatin by TAGM-MAP but not by the SVM
chrom_extra <- msn |>
  fData() |>
  filter(markers == "unknown",
         tagm.map.allocation.pred == "Chromatin",
         svm.pred == "unknown") |>
  rownames()

## Chromatin markers
chrom_markers <- featureNames(msn)[fData(msn)$markers == "Chromatin"]

## Plot profiles
plotDist(msn[c(chrom_extra, chrom_markers), ],
         markers = chrom_markers, type = "l",
         mcol = "red", pcol = "grey",
         las = 2)
title("Chromatin markers (red) and additional TAGM-MAP proteins (grey)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


Compare the shape of the grey profiles with those of the markers, in each
replicate. Then highlight `chrom_extra` on the PCA and t-SNE maps, as above,
to see where these proteins lie relative to the chromatin cluster.

:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

* Spatial maps of classification results are made with `plot2D` by passing
  the prediction column to `fcol`. Different dimensionality reduction methods
  show the data in different ways, so it is good practice to look at more
  than one.
* Pre-computing coordinates with `plot = FALSE`, using a seed for stochastic
  methods, and reusing them with `method = "none"` makes figures faster and
  reproducible.
* Proteins of interest can be found with `pRolocVis` and highlighted on any
  map with `highlightOnPlot`. Annotations such as complexes, pathways or
  compartments left out of training can be stored as new `fData` columns with
  `addMarkers` and plotted like markers.
* Scaling points by their score or probability shows the confidence of
  predictions on a map, and makes differences between classifiers visible.
* Classification results should always be checked critically by looking at
  both maps and protein profiles. These checks may lead back to the markers,
  as marker curation and classification are an iterative process.
:::
